Gut reaction: I'm on a tight budget and I'm already stressed about the half marathon, so I'd mostly pick on price and whether it fills me up. Calorie counts are the only thing that gives me usable information, because I can compare a 240 bar with a 95 fruit pot quickly. Warnings telling me obesity causes cancer feel preachy, and I'd probably just tune them out. The graphic photos might make me wince once or twice, but they wouldn't change what I can afford. They'd also be on the very things that fill me up cheaply. The counts alone, without the lecture, would nudge me most, though only a bit, since lower-calorie snacks often cost more and leave me hungry.

Gut reaction: the graphic photos would make me roll my eyes and want a bacon roll, though I'd admit a bowel tumour picture on a Dairy Milk might put me off that one bar for a minute. Plain text warnings are just wallpaper, I'd scroll past them like the smoking-kills stuff. The calorie badges are the only thing that gives me something useful, because I'd see 240 against 95 and it's not preachy, just information. But food is my treat right now, so honestly none of it shifts me much. Calories on everything would nudge me a bit, and the photos plus calories would nudge me slightly more in the moment, though I'd resent it.

My gut reaction is that the calorie badges are the only thing that gives me something to act on. I'm watching my money and I already count pennies, so counting calories on a snack is easy to picture, and seeing 240 next to 95 would make me think twice. The plain warning is just the sort of thing I'd scroll past, since "excess calories cause cancer" is the same nagging as every other campaign. The graphic photos would make me wince, and probably put me off for a day or two, but I'd get used to them quickly and resent being lectured. Photo plus calories would work a bit better than photo alone, because the numbers give me a reason to pick the fruit pot.

Gut reaction: I hate being told off, so the graphic photos would make me roll my eyes, though they'd probably stick in my head a bit more than plain text. What actually works on me is numbers. I stopped the fizzy drinks because I saw the cost and felt sluggish, not because of a warning. A calorie badge on everything lets me compare a Dairy Milk to a fruit pot at a glance and decide for myself, which suits me. The warnings add a bit on top, but they're preachy and "obesity causes cancer" is something I already know. Plain text plus calories (D) is okay, and the graphic version with calories (C) might nudge me a little more, but it'd also irritate me. F is the one I'd respond to most without feeling lectured.

My gut reaction is that the graphic photos would turn my stomach for a second, but I'd get used to them fast, like the pictures on fag packets. The calorie badge is something I'd actually use, because I'm watching my sugar and my money, and seeing "240" next to "95" is a clear, practical comparison with no lecturing. Plain text warnings by themselves I'd scroll past, since I already know crisps aren't good for me. Photos plus calories would probably have the most effect in the first week, but the calories alone feel the least preachy and the most useful day to day.

Gut reaction: I hate being nagged, so the graphic photos would irritate me most. I'd probably find them off-putting, but I'd also get used to them quickly and then resent them. The calorie badge on its own is just facts, which is what I like. I can glance at it and decide for myself, and it might make me think twice about something like the Gü dessert. Even so, I'm not changing much, because snacks aren't a big part of my eating and I don't scrimp on food.

The plain text warning is a bit preachy but easy to ignore. The graphic one might put me off a Dairy Milk in the moment, but I'd likely just feel lectured and buy it anyway. Combining the calories with the warnings adds some information, but the warning part just adds nag.

Points go mostly to C, the calorie badge alone, with a bit to E for the shock factor and to A for the calories plus plain text.

My gut reaction is that I'd mostly roll my eyes at the warnings. "Excess calories cause obesity" is preachy, and with Crohn's I'm not always trying to cut calories. Sometimes I need them, and some of those "healthy" snacks like apple crisps or a KIND bar full of nuts can set me off. Graphic photos of a bowel tumour would be upsetting rather than motivating, and I'd probably just look away, though they'd have a bit more effect than plain text, which I'd scroll past.

The calorie badge is neutral and just information. It would nudge me slightly when I'm choosing between two things, and it's the least patronising option. But I'm not a calorie counter, so the effect would be small. Honestly, the vending machine choice comes down to hunger, my gut that day, and the price.

I'd give the most points to the ones with calories on everything (E, D), a bit more to the graphic-plus-calories option (C) because it's the strongest overall, and little to the plain warning alone or the unlabelled option.
